lead: A tanning mitt is a thin glove, typically velvet-like on the outside and sometimes lined with latex or another barrier on the inside, used to spread self-tanning product across the skin and keep the user's hands from being coloured. People use it to get a smooth, even sunless tan on the face and body without stained palms, streaky patches or orange fingertips, which is why it is part of the standard self-tan kit.[1][4]

The mitt has no tanning action of its own. Colour comes from the sunless tanner, whose active ingredient, dihydroxyacetone (DHA), reacts with amino acids in the dead outer skin layer and does not need UV light.[2][4] Products typically contain 3 to 5 percent DHA, and lotion-based colour fades gradually over roughly 3 to 10 days as the outer skin sheds.[4]

Self-tanning is a way to look bronzed without sun exposure: the FDA regulates DHA as a cosmetic colour additive for external use only, and reviews advise keeping it away from the eyes, lips and mucous membranes.[2][3][4] No published study has tested tanning mitts; their benefits for evenness come from product use and community experience.

chain: Even, thin layer of DHA on skin, hands stay clean
Smooth, natural-looking tan without streaks or stained palms
angle.text: The mitt helps apply sunless tanner in a thin, even layer and prevents the hands from turning orange, giving a more natural, uniform-looking tan.

infobox: Washable or replaceable; residue can build up

paras: Sunless tanners come as lotions, gels, mousses, sprays, wipes and drops. Applying them by hand leaves colour on the palms and between the fingers, because DHA also reacts with the keratin of the hands; a mitt separates the hand from the product.[1][2]
Spray tanning, by hand-held airbrush or in an automated booth, is the other common application route and does not use a mitt.[4]

The mitt spreads product in a thin layer through a smoothing, circular motion, and a barrier lining blocks contact between the hand and product. This follows from how DHA behaves on skin, since the colour forms in the outermost dead skin layer.[1][2] Wikipedia describes DHA as 'not a dye, stain or paint' and says the browning is a Maillard-type reaction.[4]

Eva Wittgenstein discovered DHA's browning effect in the 1950s at Cincinnati Children's Hospital; the first commercial DHA self-tanner, Man-Tan, appeared in 1959 and Coppertone's QT in 1960, both with orange-toned results. Reformulations and spray-tan booths from the late 1990s broadened the market.[4]

The accessory itself is not associated with documented harm. Sunless tanning reviews cite irritant or allergic contact dermatitis from DHA products, and note that tanners do not provide sun protection.[2][3][4] The FDA approves DHA for external use only, not around the eyes or lips or by inhalation.[4]

Mitts appear in tanning routines as part of the standard kit with a self-tanning mousse or lotion, alongside exfoliation beforehand. Tanned skin is treated as a quick cosmetic improvement to complexion and facial contrast.
No studies found of tanning mitts. Research on DHA itself is covered in reviews of sunless tanning, including a 2023 review of its properties and safety and a 2018 review of the compound.[2][3]
